positions.commentary: The industry remains hit-driven, meaning that despite maturity, new surprises like Fortnite are still possible.
Take-Two's mobile business is a declining asset with no pipeline to offset weaknesses, making it a strategic liability.

thesis: The episode argues that EA possesses a stable, recurring revenue model driven by core franchises like FIFA and Star Wars, though its mobile business faces significant headwinds from privacy issues and declining user acquisition efficiency. Conversely, Take-Two is viewed as a strategic liability due to its declining mobile assets and lack of a pipeline to offset weaknesses. The analysis suggests that while EA has successfully consolidated and reinvested in new studios, investors must weigh the risks of high expectations for titles like GTA against the industry's inherent hit-driven nature.

claims.claim: EA has a stable, ongoing business with loyal customers and predictable growth driven by franchises like FIFA.
claims.quote: EA has grown FIFA over the last decade every year, some higher than others, but it's still like this ongoing business. They have this core group of people that are continuing to spend and have complete loyalty.

claims.claim: Take-Two's mobile business is a declining asset with no pipeline to offset weaknesses, making it a strategic liability.
claims.quote: And the key thing here is they have absolutely no capability of building new games within Zinga. And this is the critical point is that they do not have extra teams building new stuff. They have no pipeline whatsoever to offset the weaknesses in their core businesses.

claims.claim: EA's content is mostly licensed, making it harder for a buyer like Amazon to acquire compared to Take-Two.
claims.quote: EA is a little bit different in the sense that majority of their content is licensed, most of their biggest content, so it's a little bit harder.

claims.claim: EA's CEO hates mobile generally speaking, similar to how Take-Two's leadership views the platform.
claims.quote: similar to the way EA, the CEO of EA, hates mobile, generally speaking.

claims.claim: EA is praised for being smart to reinvest revenue into building new game teams and acquiring studios like Respawn.
claims.quote: EA did the smart thing. They bought respawn, right? And they bought that management team and that group. And Vincent Bell, he's an amazing operator and studio leader, which is the hardest roles to fill within these type of organizations.

claims.claim: EA has successfully created multiple studios under Vincent Bell that are creating AAA content including Star Wars and Black Panther games.
claims.quote: He's created like four or five studios under him that are actually creating AAA content, including the Star Wars game, including the Black Panther game and the Iron Man game. They're working on a metal honor game.

claims.claim: EA is described as having consolidated to fewer franchises and focusing on revenue per user rather than making tons of games.
claims.quote: Historically, when I was the first at EA, we were building like 30 games a year. Now, if they do six games, that's a lot. And again, the focus has been on revenue per user as opposed to tons of games trying to expand the audience.

claims.claim: EA's mobile business is facing issues with core businesses falling apart due to IDFA and privacy issues.
claims.quote: The problem is, is that all those core businesses are falling apart right now because IDFA and all these privacy issues. And Take 2 bought this company at the peak.

claims.claim: EA's mobile games like Candy Crush are at 40% margins for individual products that scale.
claims.quote: So for individual products that scale, absolutely. So for something like Kings, Candy Crush, I think they are at 40% margins, and certain big games do scale in that way.

claims.claim: EA's mobile business is consolidating amongst big publishers and big games due to expensive user acquisition costs.
claims.quote: But my opinion of mobile has changed now is that user acquisition cost is so expensive. Game development is getting more and more expensive. But you spend more on user acquisition than you do on game development, right, which is not the case for console.

claims.claim: EA's mobile business has cornerstones that are generating all the profit and revenue but are falling apart due to privacy issues.
claims.quote: And Zenga does have some amazing games that they've acquired over the years. And so those are like the cornerstones of their business in terms of what's generating all the profit and the revenue for that matter. The problem is, is that all those core businesses are falling apart right now because IDFA and all these privacy issues.

claims.claim: EA's mobile business was acquired by Take 2 at the peak.
claims.quote: And Take 2 bought this company at the peak.

claims.claim: EA's mobile business is consolidating to fewer and fewer franchises.
claims.quote: And the game makers have just consolidated to fewer and fewer and fewer franchises.

claims.claim: EA's mobile business is evolving in a winner take-all type thing where certain types of genres are the main revenue drivers of the business.
claims.quote: And mobile is evolving in that way, too, where it is almost a winner take-all type thing where certain types of genres are the main revenue drivers of the business.

claims.claim: EA's mobile business has been the way it's been since almost 2014.
claims.quote: And that's been the way it's been since almost 2014.

claims.claim: EA's mobile business is consolidating to a few studios.
claims.quote: Gaming is no different than even movies and television, which kind of consolidated to a few studios, right, or to a few networks until Netflix came out, and then that changed the game, right? A new platform game and created much more opportunity.

claims.claim: EA has successfully transformed its business model with predictable recurring revenue from core franchises like FIFA and 2K.
claims.quote: EA has grown FIFA over the last decade every year, some higher than others, but it's still like this ongoing business. They have this core group of people that are continuing to spend and have complete loyalty. 2K is the same thing.

claims.claim: The speaker warns that high expectations for GTA could be a risk due to a smaller install base and potential user burnout.
claims.quote: My biggest worry is that people's expectations on GTA get ahead of themselves. People have to keep in mind that the install base is a lot lower that they're selling selling into. The total address over market is smaller.

claims.claim: The industry remains hit-driven, meaning that despite maturity, new surprises like Fortnite are still possible.
claims.quote: Clearly, you have to focus on the businesses that make up the majority of their earnings, right? So keep an eye on the big titles, GTA and 2K, similar EA, similar actors, etc. And then also, you got to keep an eye on the potential downsides of businesses that aren't doing well, like Zingo.
